articles.title: Keelon Russell vs. Kamario Taylor: College football's next great quarterback duel?
articles.summary: Two 19-year-old quarterbacks are turning Alabama-Mississippi State into one of the most intriguing games of the college football season.
articles.body:
Hey, here's a novel concept in 2026: looking forward to a college football game that will involve football players doing football things. No congressional hearings, no wandering coaches, no pearl-clutching over NIL, no playoff expansion talk, just straight-up ball led by two of the best doing it right now.

Saturday at noon eastern, No. 7 Alabama travels to No. 16 Mississippi State in the latest installment of a rivalry that dates to the 19th century. Alabama owns the rivalry, 86-18-3, but old history isn't the story this weekend; the bright future is.

Two of the most exciting quarterbacks of the 2026 season, Alabama's Keelon Russell and Mississippi State 's Kamario Taylor , will face off in a game likely to produce offensive fireworks on both sides of the ball. Russell and Taylor took different paths from high school to meet on Saturday — one was a nationally-known prodigy, the other a local hero — but now they've both arrived on the big stage.

As a high schooler in Dallas, Russell was named the 2024 Gatorade High School Player of the Year, an honor previously won by Peyton Manning , Kyler Murray and Jaxson Dart , among other future pros. He committed to SMU, but current Falcons quarterback Michael Penix Jr. helped convince him to flip his commitment to Alabama and Penix's former coach, Kalen DeBoer.

At Alabama, Russell sat for a year behind future first-round NFL pick Ty Simpson , then won the starting job just days before the beginning of the season. In four wins this year, he's already thrown for 1,129 yards at an 8-to-2 touchdown-to-interception ratio, and he's rushed for another three touchdowns.

"Incredibly accurate," Mississippi State head coach Jeff Lebby said of Russell. "They're taking care of the football. They've got a lot of different weapons. They're good at running back as well. And so you see a guy that is really playing well beyond his years right now."

Taylor, on the other hand, grew up in tiny Macon, Mississippi, 45 minutes south of Starkville. A four-star quarterback out of Noxubee County High School, he got his first start last year in the Egg Bowl. In one hell of a trial by fire against then-No. 6 Ole Miss, Taylor showed out, rushing for 173 yards and two touchdowns and throwing for another 178 yards.

Coming into the 2026 season, Taylor was the undisputed starter for Mississippi State, and in four wins, he's thrown 14 touchdowns against just two interceptions. His signature moment so far: rallying Mississippi State to two touchdowns and a comeback 31-24 win inside the final four minutes against Missouri last week.

"He's got a tremendous deep ball, but I think he's got the other areas of the game, too, and does a good job managing the game within their scheme and within their system," DeBoer said this week. "And he's got the ability to run and extend plays with his legs, too. Extremely talented, I mean, great athlete."

There's a slight difference in motivation in play this weekend. Mississippi State, No. 16 in both the AP and Coaches' polls, is ranked for the first time since 2022. That makes this weekend's game against the No. 7 Tide the most important one the Bulldogs have played in years. A win here legitimizes the program's ascent — and probably ensures the 19-year-old Taylor won't ever buy a drink in Starkville … once he's old enough, of course.

Alabama, on the other hand, has a larger pack of Bulldogs in mind — the ones from Georgia, who head to Tuscaloosa next weekend. No one's suggesting that the Tide are overlooking Mississippi State — that's the fastest way to get upset — but let's just say that Alabama wasn't circling the Mississippi State date on the calendar the moment it was announced.

Both coaches face a significant challenge in dealing with the other's star QB, but both are taking a remarkably similar approach: see if you can get the 19-year-old to remember he's 19 years old.

"He looks very calm. And a guy that looks like he's in complete command," Lebby said of Russell. "We're gonna have to move him off the spot."

"We just have to try to do everything we can to make … the quarterback uncomfortable as possible," DeBoer said, "and try to keep them off schedule."

Speaking of schedules: Alabama's taking a slightly unconventional approach to gameday planning, opting to drive the entire 85 miles to Starkville the morning of the game. Factoring in tailgate traffic — and the possibility that a Mississippi State trooper will spot a possible busted taillight on the team bus — that means the Tide will be up with the sunrise, rolling up Highway 82.

DeBoer delicately suggested that the lack of appropriate hotel facilities in the Starkville area led Alabama — and other programs — to stay in T-Town. "Other teams have been staying here in Tuscaloosa recently as they come through heading up that way," DeBoer said this week. "Again, it's been done before. Just as recently as three years ago. It worked then." (That was a 40-17 Alabama victory, during the final head-coaching season of that other guy.)

Regardless of which side of the Mississippi-Alabama state line you favor, there's one element of this weekend's marquee quarterback matchup we can all appreciate: no matter what, we've got at least one more year of watching these two 19-year-olds in college after this season. The NFL scouts in attendance at Saturday's game won't be able to get their hooks in either quarterback until the 2028 draft.

Maybe we're looking at the first duel of a duet that will be linked together in football history, the Brady-Manning of the 2030s and 2040s. And maybe these two will portal their way to different schools and different fates by this time next year, never to cross paths again. But none of that matters on Saturday. What we'll have then is two football teams, two fan bases, focused entirely on football. For a change.

articles.summary: Confira as agendas de Professora Dorinha (União) e Du Pereira (DC).
articles.body:
Confira a agenda de campanha dos candidatos ao governo do Tocantins nesta sexta-feira (2). Professor Witer Naves (PSOL), Ataídes de Oliveira (NOVO) e Vicentinho Júnior (PSDB) não tiveram compromissos públicos de campanha hoje. A candidata Professora Dorinha (União Brasil) teve encontro com representantes dos servidores públicos em Palmas e Du Pereira (DC), visitou os comércios da capital.

📱 Clique aqui para seguir o canal do g1 TO no WhatsApp

Professora Dorinha (União) e Du Pereira (DC) — Foto: Reprodução/TV Anhanguera

A candidata pelo União Brasil, cumpriu agenda no gabinete. Nesta reta final de campanha, ela realizou uma série de reuniões. O principal encontro foi com a Liga Sindical Tocantinense, entidade que representa diversas categorias de servidores públicos do estado. A candidata assinou uma carta de compromisso com os pedidos apresentados pelo grupo.

"Diminuindo essa diferença. Porque não tem justificativa, às vezes, para a mesma função ou situações em que a pessoa tá exposta a situação insalubre ou até de insegurança e não tem nenhum tipo de benefício e uma outra tem. Não é tirar de quem tem, é olhar quem tem a necessidade, de acordo com a atribuição, e não é uma coisa de escolha. Muitas delas são reguladas legalmente, que precisam ser ajustadas. Nós vamos fazer isso", afirmou a candidata.

O candidato do partido Democracia Cristã, caminhou junto com apoiadores na região sul de Palmas. O candidato destacou a necessidade do governo do estado trabalhar junto com a prefeitura.

"O acesso que vai ter aqui para trazer benefício para a população é a prefeitura. Então o governo do estado precisa fazer parceria com a prefeitura para que melhore a vida de quem convive aqui no Taquari, que é um dos maiores bairros da nossa do nosso estado, né? A minha campanha foi mais voltada para a região sul de Palmas e para o interior, onde precisa de mais acessibilidade no nosso estado.

articles.title: 'G7 strikes oil deal' and Alison's TV heart scare'
articles.summary: G7 countries have agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel after an export ban threat by Donald Trump.
articles.body:
Spoiler warning: This press review reveals details from series two of The Celebrity Traitors.

The Sun leads on the terror charges brought against the man accused of killing Reform UK spokeswoman Ann Widdecombe. The paper says the police are linking Joshua Kerry to an alleged firebomb attack on the party leader, Nigel Farage's home last year. "Ann suspect on Nigel terror rap" reads its headline.

The Times says the price of diesel at the pump is expected to fall, after European leaders struck a deal with Donald Trump to release emergency stockpiles of fuel. The report says that would avert a US export ban, previously threatened by the President.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch says her party would cut foreign aid to pay for 50,000 new jail cells, according to the Daily Mail . The paper calls it the biggest prison-building programme since the Victorian era.

The Daily Telegraph says the United Arab Emirates has threatened to pull billions of pounds of investment out of the UK, in retaliation for Manchester City being found to have broken Premier League financial rules. Its report says in the weeks before the verdict was announced the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, held a meeting with the club's chairman, but the Department for Business insists the two men didn't discuss football.

The Financial Times says Chancellor John Healey's first Budget this month is expected to provide "breathing space" for households and businesses, rather than impose tax rises. The paper says big decisions have been parked until next year and that Labour insiders have said Healey's main aim is to reassure investors. One senior party figure is quoted as saying "it won't be a blow-the-doors-off budget".

School inspections in England will be changed for the second time in a year according to the Guardian . The paper says the new system - introduced after the death of a headteacher - has received a barrage of complaints that it's damaging school leaders' mental health. Education Secretary Lucy Powell will reportedly tell the regulator, Ofsted, to "go back to the drawing board".

The Daily Mirror leads on what it calls the TV presenter, Alison Hammond's "heart scare". The 51-year-old was rushed off air after clutching her chest during This Morning yesterday. Its front-page features a picture of Hammond in her hospital bed, who later said she was getting her "old ticker checked out".

images.caption: The G7 striking an oil deal with Donald Trump features in today's papers. The Times reports on the agreement by G7 countries to release 100 million barrels of "emergency stockpiles of fuel and avert a US export ban". "The price of diesel at the pump is expected to fall", the paper says, after countries including France, Germany and Italy agreed to release a "massive amount" of diesel to ease supply pressures. The US president had warned he would ban diesel exports from the US if European countries did not offer up more of their own stocks onto the market.

articles.title: India vs Brazil: Khalid Jamil’s Blue Tigers face biggest test yet in Kolkata
articles.summary: KOLKATA: Two teams navigating turbulent periods of transition, a few routines taking the back seat and new ideas taking shape; some old hands like Sunil
articles.body: KOLKATA: Two teams navigating turbulent periods of transition, a few routines taking the back seat and new ideas taking shape; some old hands like Sunil Chhetri here and Neymar there riding off into the sunset and new faces ready to take the journey forward. However, the comparison between Brazil and India ahead of their momentous meeting at Salt Lake Stadium on Saturday looks to end before it even promises to start a debate.A mismatch? Thrust into a challenge like a lamb to the slaughter? Or ready to play with fire? The Blue Tigers’ face-off with the highest FIFA-ranked rivals can offer one an invitation to absorb the story with diverse perspectives. At the core, though, lies the need to press the reset button.During his long managerial career, Carlo Ancelotti has supervised several rebuilding processes. At Brazil, it’s a different ball game for him though.“Training a club is a different job, but with the national team, you have to be more focused on the selection of the players,” Ancelotti told the TOI during his pre-match press conference on Friday. “We have more time to do the right things. It is very special to have the time to train every day with the Brazilian players.”PSG defender Marquinhos, who is set to lead Brazil in absence of Barcelona’s injured star Raphinha, echoed the sentiment.“Football is extremely competitive. We can’t always win, and that is part of the game, he said.“There are other great teams, and there will sometimes be frustration. But we keep fighting with character and charisma.”With odds heavily stacked against the hosts, India coach Khalid Jamil also gave his own perspective on this somewhat linear trajectory, harping on the anything-can-happen belief in football. He has stirred up a hornet’s nest by wielding his axe on several senior players for the three friendlies in this FIFA window and it’s time now to vindicate the move. It has started well with a credible 1-1 draw with Panama but Brazil will be a different challenge.“Am I losing sleep over this? Surely, pressure is there and we must take pressure. It’s going to be one of our best games and we must be prepared to perform and rise to the challenge,” Jamil said.It will be a dream come true moment for many of the Indian team sharing the pitch with the Brazilians on Saturday. articles.title: Pitt beats Virginia Tech 35-33 after Hokies' game-winning field goal appears to go over an upright
articles.summary: John Love missed his 36-yard attempt by mere inches.
articles.body:
Pitt hung on for a 35-33 win over Virginia Tech on Friday night after John Love missed a game-winning 36-yard field goal as time expired.

Love's kick certainly looked like it snuck inside the left upright from ESPN's live broadcast feed. But the official directly underneath the upright ruled that it didn't go through, much to Love's chagrin.

The circumstances of the kick have become commonplace in college football. As kickers have become better, there are more instances of the ball going through — or appearing to go through — the uprights at a height higher than the goal posts. And that's where the judgment of the officials on the ground comes into play.

Per the NCAA's rules, the entire football must be in between the inside of the uprights when it passes between the posts. If a ball travels over the upright — as it might have done in this case — it's no good. Consider it like a kick that bounces off an upright and not over the crossbar.

Furthermore, it's a play that isn't reviewed. The only extra point and field-goal attempts that can be reviewed are kicks that are lower than the height of the uprights. You can review a kick that went inside or outside the posts if it's 3 feet below the top of the uprights. You can't review a kick that went 3 inches above the uprights.

It was an odd ending to what turned out to be an odd game. Virginia Tech turned the ball over four times in the loss and Pitt lost quarterback Mason Heintschel to what looks to be a serious right knee injury. Heintschel was injured when he got hit while scrambling and immediately grabbed his knee. He was unable to put any pressure on that leg after the play, and returned to the sideline in street clothes after exiting the game.

Pitt scored 21 straight points to take a 35-24 lead in the fourth quarter, but an interception by Virginia Tech QB Ethan Grunkemeyer near the Pitt end zone quickly turned into a safety and then the Hokies cut the lead to two on their next drive.

Pitt is now 5-0 and should be ranked in the AP Top 25 when the new poll is released Sunday even if Heintschel is out for an extended period of time. He was replaced by Holden Geriner, who was 8-of-12 passing for 78 yards and a TD, and three different Pitt players rushed for a touchdown in the win.

articles.title: Brazil at the Mecca of Indian Football: A Dream Fixture, But Is Indian Football Paying the Price?
articles.summary: As the weekend of the year commences, the Indian men’s football team take on five-time World Champions Brazil at the Mecca of Indian football, the Salt
articles.body: As the weekend of the year commences, the Indian men’s football team take on five-time World Champions Brazil at the Mecca of Indian football, the Salt Lake Stadium in Kolkata - a city that’s hosted Pele, albeit not in the Selecao yellow.Brazil exited the 2026 World Cup with a Round of 16 loss and are restarting another cycle. They’ve always had the luxury of the spotlight. India’s footballing journey is entering yet another cycle too, but that’s for the back burner — a term often heard in the various corridors of power. Nonetheless, Khalid Jamil’s players aren’t exactly short on confidence. Whatever happens, the games against Brazil and Uruguay will probably rank very high on the list of highlights for Khalid and his players, and enjoy it they must!The positivity in the camp stems from a relatively good showing against Panama in a 1-1 draw in Bangalore, at the Kanteerava Stadium, a venue that’s not alien to special nights. However, the Kanteerava Stadium, which can become a cauldron, thanks largely to the West Block Blues, wasn’t even half full, because dirty seats and expensive tickets don’t go hand in hand. The Kanteerava is a 26,000-seater stadium which saw 9,000 people attend the game against World No. 44 Panama. The West Block Blues normally shell out anywhere between INR 400-700 for Indian Super League games, whereas the cheapest tickets for the Panama game were INR 849 and the seats in the West Block Blues’ stand were priced at INR 2,999.Next on the playlist is Kolkata, a city known for its love for Brazil’s football team. Ahead of the festivities of Durga Puja, even the Mecca of Indian football took some time to warm up. The reason is probably squarely down to the ticket prices. And the All India Football Federation weren’t particularly keen on being consumer-friendly. Dismal ticket sales, though, forced their hand, and out came the 1+1 ticket schemes. In Kolkata, most ISL games would not cost you above a maximum of INR 500, and the tickets for the two friendlies start at INR 999. The cheapest tickets in Kolkata are generally INR 100 for domestic matches.ALSO READ | India vs Brazil: Khalid Jamil’s Blue Tigers face biggest test yet in KolkataThe red carpet versus the reality of Indian footballHere’s the thing: the AIFF, the body responsible for football and its development in the country, currently led by Kalyan Chaubey, is tasked with waking up the "Sleeping Giant of world football" - a term coined by former FIFA President Sepp Blatter in 2007. Almost two decades later, Carlo Ancelotti says India doesn’t have a football culture. Is he completely wrong to say so?Which serves as a better alarm clock? Friendlies (that cost a bomb) versus Panama, Brazil and Uruguay, or simply growing the game?It isn’t that the friendlies won’t attract attention for those few days, but is that cutting your coat according to your cloth? You could probably live near the Governor's House in Mumbai or somewhere around Lord’s with the amount of money that is reportedly being spent on these games. A report in Mint suggests a total budget of INR 90 crore for three matches. One hopes the accounts teams have taken a leaf out of Florentino Perez’s playbook because otherwise, we could be in for a steep trek on the mountain of debt.Imagine being the first set of AIFF officials to bring Brazil to India for a football match that becomes a part of the record books. The President and his entourage get their photos, their moments under the floodlights, and coincidentally, all of this happens before the top post is up for election in December. It was earlier slated for September.After all, coincidence and every other word you can think of are all part of the English language and dictionary. We don’t do other languages, and the words might change in a few sentences.ALSO READ | Once bitten, twice shy: How Kolkata is gearing up for India vs Brazil after Lionel Messi fiascoMind you, India’s draw against Panama has attracted international attention, in terms of media, and the games against Brazil and Uruguay surely will as well. But what is the lasting impact on Indian football? Or is the plan just to have a few moments of merriment?Three friendlies cannot fix Indian footballIf the AIFF had taken the development of football seriously, the money being spent on these friendlies could have and should have been parked solely for the Indian football ecosystem, where clubs struggling for finance is not uncommon, and not long ago, players were pleading to save domestic top-flight football, which was in grave danger. Thankfully, there is light at the end of the tunnel for the top flight.Indian football has seen some great days. In the first two decades just after Independence, the Indian football team were among the best in Asia, but since then, the team has tapered off, and how! There was a time when India were considered to be the Brazil of Asia.Three friendlies will not change the reality, and the hurdles that the ecosystem faces will not magically disappear. What may disappear is a few fans, a few kids who decide not to take up the sport because their parents don’t see a proper career path. When clubs shut down with alarming regularity and the football calendar faces commercial issues every now and then, every parent would be wary of letting their kid take up football as a first-choice career in India.The AIFF chose the red carpet over addressing the reality of the sport within our country. Every few years, a new dawn arrives. articles.title: Ranking Sunderland’s Top Ten Greatest Managers Of All Time
articles.summary: From Watson and Stokoe to Le Bris, who’s Sunderland’s greatest ever boss? Lewis Forbister has his say!
articles.body:
It's often discussed by people at the match, in pubs, houses and on social media: who's their club's greatest manager of all time? I feel like when discussing best players, it's easier to go off goals and appearances, but debating the best manager is, in my opinion, is a topic of conversation with more to it.

From Tom Watson to Régis Le Bris, Johnny Cochrane to Peter Reid, who's the greatest gaffer to have led Sunderland AFC? Here's is my top ten.

McCarthy took the helm from Howard Wilkinson in 2003, getting the club to an FA Cup semi-final in the process.

The season after, he would guide the club to the newly named EFL Championship title, His tenure would end in 2006, and he would then go on to manage Wolverhampton Wanderers.

Brown managed the club to a Second Division title in 1963/1964 following the club's first ever relegation in 1963.

Charlie Hurley led the Lads on the pitch, but Brown was the mastermind off it and he would also take Sunderland on a run to the FA Cup quarter-finals, beating Northampton Town, Bristol City and Everton on our way to facing Manchester United in a face-off that took three matches to decide.

A 3-3 draw at Old Trafford on 29 February 1964 meant the game would be replayed at Roker Park, which would end 2-2 on 4 March. So, the next match had to be held at a neutral ground, which was Elland Road on 9 March, where the Black Cats went down to a valiant and battling defeat to the Red Devils.

Brown and the Lads' focus immediately turned back to the league, in which they confirmed promotion at the first time of asking back to the top flight just a few weeks later.

Keane arrived at Sunderland with the club rooted to the bottom of the Championship following relegation from the Premier League.

We were candidates to go down to League One in the autumn of 2007, and we were champions in the spring of 2007, with the Irishman laying the foundations for Sunderland to enjoy an uninterrupted decade-long spell at England's top table.

He had us promoted as champions in 2006/2007, guided us to a comfortable fifteenth-placed finish in 2007/2008 and would depart in December 2008, but the groundwork he completed helped the club massively throughout the next few years.

Mackie guided Sunderland as to their fourth league title as player-manager during the 1901/1902 campaign after finishing second the season before. He placed the Rokerites among the elite again, overseeing a resurgence following the quiet years between 1898 and 1901.

A financial scandal in 1905 would push Mackie out of the club and into the arms of Middlesbrough, where he spent one year on Teesside before moving into hotel ownership.

Kyle was in charge on Wearside for a monumental twenty three years between 1905 and 1923 and still remains the longest-serving Sunderland manager to date. His crowning achievement was winning the 1912/1913 First Division — Sunderland's fifth title.

He would also take the Lads to the 1913 FA Cup final but would unfortunately miss out against a strong Aston Villa side.

Reid took over at Sunderland in March 1995, with the club sitting in twentieth place in the First Division.

The following season, he had a full campaign to get the Lads pushing on, and he did, winning the 1995/1996 First Division title with eighty three points and giving us Mackems a first taste of Premier League football.

However, it would be an immediate return to the second tier, with Reid remaining at the helm to take Sunderland back up to the Premier League in the 1998/1999 campaign, winning our third second-tier title with a record 105 points — a record which has only ever been beaten once.

This time around, there were no fears of relegation; in fact, it was quite the opposite as Reid had Sunderland second in the Premier League by Christmas 1999 and would eventually finish seventh come May 2000. The same feat would be achieved the following campaign, with the Black Cats fighting for the European places for two years, missing out on goal difference in 2000 and then by four points in 2001.

The man from Merseyside allowed Mackems to start to dream again, and he's held in such high regard by supporters past and present due to his style of football and the players he brought in, such as the legendary strike partnership of Niall Quinn and Kevin Phillips, the latter winning the European Golden Shoe in 2000.

Reid would also sign Stefan Schwarz and Don Hutchinson to boost a conceivable top-half push.

Le Bris arrived at the Stadium of Light in July 2024 following a dismal 2023/2024 campaign that saw Sunderland under the guidance of three managers and a bleak sixteenth-placed finish, yet what followed was truly unpredictable.

In his first twenty three Championship games, he lost just three and had Sunderland sitting second in the league on Boxing Day.

A 'derby' double over Middlesbrough and a playoff campaign that will be remembered for generations followed — Coventry City were the opponents, and Sunderland would travel to the CBS, winning 2-1 and leading going into the second leg.

It was a cagey game back at the Stadium of Light but Le Bris' tactics saw the Black Cats hold on until the 121st minute, when there was plenty of movement inside the box…

Dan Ballard sent Sunderland to Wembley at the death, and this was a make-or-break moment for Le Bris as Wembley beckoned and the Lads knew what was at stake. This was our year and what forty eight games had led up to.

We won the playoff final 2-1 — again, at the death, this was how Le Bris Sunderland set up during this campaign and the next: attritional, strong and not scared of any opponent.

In 2025/2026, Le Bris and the Lads achieved something unprecedented since 1973, qualification for the Europa League via a seventh-placed finish. This was our highest finish in the Premier League since 1999/2000 and 2000/2001, and Le Bris also became the eighth Sunderland manager to do the league double over our rivals on the Tyne.

He said he "won't play like Guardiola or De Zerbi because he is Régis Le Bris, and the 'Le Bris way' has brought a level of success to Wearside that's not been seen since 2001, and you could even argue 1973.

Now, I've said all this and only have Le Bris ranked fourth, and this is because he's achieved almost everything Bob Stokoe achieved: European qualification and promotion. However, the Frenchman hasn't won a major honour with Sunderland — should he do so, he'll be placed much higher on this list.

I didn't just bring the magic. It's always been here. I just came back to find it.

Stokoe would win Sunderland the 1973 FA Cup, winning us our first trophy in thirty six years and taking into European competition for the first time in our history. Additionally, he would also restore the club's top flight status by winning the 1975/1976 Second Division title, giving supporters their first taste of First Division football since 1970.

Although he left due to a poor run of results at the beginning of 1976/1977, Sunderland supporters will always see Stokoe as an undisputed legend, immortalised in bronze outside the Stadium of Light.

Another man to have won Sunderland three league titles, Cochrane would deliver these trophies over two campaigns on Wearside.

Cochrane won the 1935/1936 Division One title and would first beat Arsenal 2-1 at Roker Park to win the Charity Shield on 28 October 1936. Six months later, the men from the Wear would descend on the capital to defeat Preston North End 2-1 and bring home the 1936/1937 FA Cup.

Cochrane didn't just bring back the glory days to Sunderland — he turned us into a dominant force once again.

Watson managed Sunderland from 1889 to 1896 before departing for Liverpool.

He turned the Black Cats a dominant force during the early days of league football in the 1890s; the Lads being nicknamed 'The Team of All Talents'. He would guide Sunderland to their first three league titles in 1891/1892, 1892/1893 and 1894/1895, as well as finishing second in 1893/1894 and placing fifth in his final campaign of 1895/1896.

For six years, he made Sunderland the best and most competitive team in England and later the world, as in 1895 the Lads would take on Hearts of Midlothian in an all-champions affair for the world championship.

Sunderland went on to beat Hearts 5-3, meaning Watson's squad were crowned 'Champions of the World'. He also managed the side under the 'Team of All Talents' moniker.

Croatia enters the match managing key defensive absences but boosted by the return of veteran leadership. Legendary midfielder Luka Modrić is expected to return to the starting lineup alongside Mateo Kovačić after being rested on the bench mid-week.

In defence, manager Slaven Bilić faces a few selection headaches. Centre-back Martin Erlić is completely ruled out until mid-October due to injury, while right-back Josip Juranović is also unavailable as he recovers from an illness.

However, defender Josip Stanišić is tipped to make his return to the backline after missing out against Spain. Croatia may also blood some younger talent, with rising defensive star Luka Vušković and winger Martin Baturina heavily pushing for a spot in the opening XI.

Dominika Livaković will start in goal, protected by a backline expected to feature Joško Gvardiol.

England manager Thomas Tuchel has confirmed a clean bill of health for his traveling 24-man squad in Rijeka, though the roster is missing several regular heavyweights.

Goalkeeper Jordan Pickford is set to reclaim his spot in goal from James Trafford as part of a planned rotation strategy. In defence, Ezri Konsa has fully recovered from a recent knock and trained without issues on Friday, making him the favourite to partner Marc Guéhi at centre-back.

The Three Lions had to adapt to late squad changes, as Manchester City's Nico O'Reilly withdrew from the camp. England are also playing without high-profile stars Declan Rice, Kobbie Mainoo, Cole Palmer, and Marcus Rashford, who all withdrew before the international break.

Despite these missing names, Tuchel boasts a strong attack led by Harry Kane, supported by Jude Bellingham and Bukayo Saka.

Croatia enters this match seeking consistency following mixed results in their opening UEFA Nations League matches. They kicked off their campaign with a hard-fought 2-1 victory over Czechia in Prague but suffered a heavy 4-1 defeat against Spain in Seville. This follows a challenging summer campaign where they were beaten 4-2 by England during the group stage of the 2026 FIFA World Cup in June.

England has displayed strong momentum under Thomas Tuchel, winning three of their last five matches in all competitions. They bounced back from a narrow 3-2 opening loss against Spain with a convincing 2-0 away victory over Czechia in their last outing. The Three Lions also hold the upper hand in recent head-to-head history, having dismantled Croatia 4-2 at the World Cup just a few months ago.

articles.title: The Football Interview: Jack Wilshere on management, Mikel Arteta, Max Dowman & Luton Town
articles.summary: Luton Town manager Jack Wilshere speaks about being back where he started as an eight-year-old and the lessons he learned from his time at Arsenal.
articles.body:
The Football Interview will be available on BBC One at 12:45 BST every Saturday during the Premier League season, as well as on BBC iPlayer, BBC Football YouTube and the BBC Sport website and app.

In the seventh episode of the new season, Kelly Somers sits down with Luton Town manager Jack Wilshere.

Jack Wilshere's footballing career has gone full circle.

From starting out at Luton Town aged seven, Wilshere went on to win trophies at Arsenal and represent England at two major tournaments, before having to retire early because of injury problems and moving into coaching.

Now, he is back where he began, at Luton, this time as manager.

Sitting overlooking the pitches he used to play on as a youngster, the 34-year-old spoke to BBC Sport's Kelly Somers for The Football Interview and discussed his career - and how he hopes he can use his experiences to improve his players.

An exciting attacking midfielder with an ability to spot a pass or dribble past his opponent, Wilshere twice won the FA Cup with the Gunners.

He played in the Premier League 182 times and represented England on 34 occasions, appearing at both the World Cup in Brazil in 2014 and the European Championship in France two years later.

But injuries plagued the latter part of his career, with him announcing his retirement at only 30.

"I loved it [my career], I'm really proud," he said in the interview, which can be watched on BBC One at 12:45 BST on Saturday, 3 October.

"I got to play for my country and represent them at two major tournaments. OK, they didn't go the way we wanted them to, but I got to do it.

"I scored for my country, I played for the club I loved growing up, so pride is the biggest thing."

Watch The Football Interview on BBC Sport

On 13 October it will be one year since Wilshere became Luton boss, his first senior management role - although he had been in interim charge of Norwich City for a two-game spell at the end of the previous season.

He has already won silverware in his time with the Hatters, guiding them to the EFL Trophy, beating Stockport County 3-1 at Wembley in April in front of a crowd of nearly 50,000.

"I'm 34 now and probably could still be playing," he added. "Don't get me wrong, I loved every minute of playing, but I also really, really love this and I'm fortunate to start my [management] journey early.

"I'm really grateful to the club and the board for giving me that opportunity because they didn't need to. I was a young coach wanting to make my first step into the game."

Immediately after his playing career ended, he was invited back to Arsenal to coach their youngsters and instantly knew management and coaching was for him.

"I hear stories about people struggling in retirement and I retired on a Monday, and I was in with the [under] 18s on a Tuesday," said Wilshere. "When I first went and walked through the door to coaching, I realised this is going to take over my life, and I need to commit myself to this if I want to improve."

By that time Mikel Arteta, who had been Wilshere's Arsenal team-mate for five years, was first-team manager.

Arteta guided the Gunners to the Premier League title in 2025-26, their first time as English champions in 22 years, and Wilshere felt the Spaniard had played a vital role in developing him as a coach.

"I got to see Mikel and how he coached and the influence he was having," said Wilshere. "I would ask him questions, why he's doing certain things, and I started to fall in love with it and how he started to prepare training sessions.

"I'd get an opportunity to practice that with the 18s in the afternoon and it was something I wasn't that good at, and I felt uncomfortable at times.

"I was influenced by Mikel, but then I had to learn how to teach. I had to learn how to get that across, how to plan a session and how to get the outcomes that you wanted.

"I played under some good coaches and was quite good at understanding what a coach wants, but I never dived into 'why is he asking me to do that?' Mikel really made that clear and I was lucky enough to have a relationship where I could say, 'well, why do you want that?' And he was open enough to share it with me."

Not only did his former club Arsenal become English champions, but Wilshere gained extra satisfaction as he had coached defender Myles Lewis-Skelly, winger Ethan Nwaneri and midfielder Max Dowman during his time at the club's academy.

Wilshere was only 16 when he made his Arsenal debut, and Dowman was 15 when he first played for the Gunners senior team, with Wilshere spotting his talent early on.

"Max played for my 18s team when he was 13," added Wilshere. "I remember calling my dad because I played for the 18s when I was 14. I was like, 'was 13 too young?'

"In the first game we could clearly see that he was ready for it. And I remember calling my dad and saying, 'you need to come watch this kid'. My dad did, and my dad's very biased, as you could imagine. But even he said, 'he's better than you'."

Learning from mistakes and a viral team talk

Wilshere, who is aiming to guide Luton to promotion to the Championship this season, felt one of his managerial strengths was being able to warn his young players of the perils of professional football.

Early in his career he had been pictured drinking and smoking, leading to criticism from then Arsenal boss Arsene Wenger, but Wilshere said he learned from the experience and passes that knowledge on to his players.

"Yes, I made mistakes, but I also reflect on that," said Wilshere, who also played for Bolton, Bournemouth, West Ham and Danish side AGF. "I had a manager that had high standards and he let me know that he was disappointed, but he also gave me another chance.

"You educate them, you let them know there's a line and there's things they can't do. But also give them another chance. I believe in that."

Wilshere's man-management skills were shown when he delivered a passionate half-time team talk, , external which then went viral on social media, as Luton trailed Reading 3-1 on the opening day of this season, only to recover and clinch a dramatic 4-3 win.

"You have to build that relationship with the players," said Wilshere. "Players also want to have high standards. They want to be held accountable. Ever since day one, they've been all-in with what we've been trying to do.

"My idea is you have to work really, really hard. I want to give the players clarity in every single moment. I'd like to think I'm really hard-working, you have to be.

"You have to have a big love for the game because it takes over your life, which I do. Then if you have that blend and try and make it enjoyable for the players, there will be challenges along the way, but you're on the right path."

articles.title: Barcelona: Rodri's rise to the top
articles.summary: Rodri is already playing a key role at Barcelona after turning down Real Madrid this summer. Guillem Balague looks at his journey so far.
articles.body:
While a generation of players build personal brands and chase clicks, the Barcelona and Spain midfielder stays away from social media and avoids the spotlight, talking about tactics the way other players talk about cars.

He is, by his own admission, an introvert who happens to control football games for a living.

The 30-year-old won 12 major trophies with Man City and helped Spain to European Championship and World Cup successes.

On Saturday, he insisted his successes with Man City could not be taken away from them after the club were found guilty of breaking the majority of the 115 financial rules they were accused of breaching by the Premier League. City are set to appeal against the ruling.

He also won the Ballon d'Or in 2024 and is in contention to win it for a second time in October, a rare achievement for a holding midfielder.

From a Connecticut summer camp through a Castellon lecture hall to a Champions League final, Rodri has shown the willingness to absorb whatever the environment demands, understand why it is being asked of him - and get on with it.

Understanding his temperament and character is also the starting point for understanding why Barcelona, not Real Madrid, is where his career has turned next after leaving Man City in the summer.

Rodri believes in Man City's 'innocence'

Heartbreak to Champions League redemption

Rodri's game was shaped by an education system that treats football intelligence as something to be taught and moulded.

Spanish academies function on the idea that a coach is a teacher first, and Rodri absorbed that from a young age. But he also came out of his comfort zone very early.

At 14, his father wanted him to spend a year at an American high school, but a season in Villarreal's youth ranks made that impossible, so the family found a compromise: a summer camp deep in the Connecticut woods.

That stay left him with the fluent, American-tinged English his Manchester City team-mates would later tease him about, and it is where he watched Spain win the 2010 World Cup, alone by a lake, thousands of miles from home.

His learning accelerated after being released by Atletico Madrid as a teenager, as his body had not caught up with his footballing brain.

Villarreal picked him up, and there the two strands of his life - football and study - ran in parallel. He moved to Castellon, the biggest city near Villarreal, at 17, and enrolled at university to study business administration.

He combined training in the morning with lectures in the afternoon. He cycled to training and lived among students who had no idea their quiet classmate would soon be starting in La Liga.

When he appeared on television one evening, his flatmates realised the boy from accounting class wore the number six shirt for Villarreal. He has since called that period the best of his life.

The rest of his rise is well known. Atletico brought him back in 2018 under Diego Simeone, who sharpened his intensity and competitiveness.

A year later, Manchester City paid his 70m euro release clause, and Guardiola turned him into arguably the finest holding midfielder of his generation.

There were setbacks, including a Champions League final defeat by Chelsea in 2021 that left him unable to speak to his own family afterwards. Two years later came the redemption, the goal that won City the Champions League in 2023.

That goal changed the story of his career. The Euros with Spain came and the Ballon d'Or followed, along with the World Cup title and MVP award that preceded his move to Barcelona this summer.

And you get the feeling his story is far from finished.

Why Rodri turned down Real Madrid for Barcelona

Rodri has been open about how seriously he took Real Madrid's interest in him this summer.

Speaking to Spanish sports radio station COPE, he said the club behaved impeccably and pursued him properly from the first approach.

He spoke to many in and around the club, and admitted the warmth of those conversations made his eventual decision harder.

New manager Jose Mourinho communicated his footballing idea clearly and what he wanted from Rodri personally, and that approach appealed to him.

Inside Real, the sense that Rodri was the player they needed went well beyond the coach.

Several figures at the club still regard him as the profile the squad is missing now, a controlling midfielder capable of dictating tempo in a way nobody currently on the books quite replicates.

The scale of Mourinho's pursuit reflected a genuine conviction that Rodri was required. Madrid have not gone out and found an alternative version of what he would have given them, so the gap the midfielder would have filled remains a gap.

Rodri's reasons for turning that interest down was footballing rather than personal.

His decision came down to where he could grow and contribute most, a project built around a squad full of young players, many of whom he knew already, and who fitted the way he understands the game.

It was a decision about which team needed what he offers, and where he could make the biggest difference.

Rodri is a footballing encyclopaedia and, many would argue, the best defensive midfielder in the world.

There are few better when it comes to positional play, and he is one of the very best because of what he does himself and what he brings out in his team-mates.

Without the ball, both in the press and when dropping back, he gives that sense of security in front of the defence, especially in those moments when Barcelona lose the ball.

But he is also outstanding with the ball because he distributes it quickly and always chooses the right route. You can see all that in every Barcelona game.

His arrival has been described inside the club as one of the most significant developments of recent years on and off the pitch - playing in all but one match of Barcelona's perfect start to the campaign.

For a squad that lost several senior voices in recent seasons, Rodri's experience in high-pressure moments has added a stability that had been missing.

He has taken on an informal mentoring role with the club's academy graduates, several of whom already regard him as a reference point.

He explains rather than simply demonstrates, an instinct that has surprised the coaching staff as much as his football has.

He does not wear the captain's armband, and probably will not for some time, but inside the dressing room many already talk about him as a captain in everything but title.

Boss Hansi Flick made clear from day one that Barcelona had signed a type of midfielder they did not have, but also a reference point for a squad in the middle of rebuilding.

His partnership with Pedri has emerged as one of the more encouraging signs, as there were doubts about it.

The two combine naturally, managing tempo and sharing the responsibility for circulating the ball. Flick sees them capable of controlling matches through positioning, possession and reading of the game rather than athleticism.

Asked to compare Flick with Guardiola, Rodri was unambiguous: they are nothing alike.

He has spoken about arriving at Barcelona expecting rondos and possession drills, only to be met with days of gruelling physical work in the gym.

Guardiola trusted competition to build match sharpness. Flick has taken a different route with the players who arrived later in pre-season, working them hard from the outset.

And as you would expect from his CV and personality, Rodri has adapted to it rather than resisted it.

articles.title: Too quiet for too long, can McGinn recapture best for Scotland?
articles.summary: Fifth in the all-time scoring chart for Scotland and closing in on 100 caps, John McGinn could do with finding his best stuff again, writes Tom English.
articles.body:
In Skopje these past few days it's been difficult to figure out the most devout people - the local followers of the city's most sacred daughter, Mother Teresa, or the arriving Scots and their most cherished son, Saint John McGinn.

Faith in the blessed one is absolute (and the same goes for Teresa). Raise a critical note and you could be shot down in flames. Point out that McGinn's talismanic excellence has been on the wane in international football for a little while now and you're liable to reap a whirlwind.

This is a weekend when Andy Robertson wins his 100th cap, but McGinn isn't far behind.

After Saturday night he'll be on 92, third on the all-time appearance list while currently sitting in fifth in the all-time scoring chart, one behind the immortal Lawrie Reilly.

There is something to be said, though, and you say it with the hesitancy of a bomb disposal expert approaching a suspect device. For Scotland, McGinn could do with finding his best stuff again.

When he arrives to chat at the Todor Proeski Stadium in Skopje he is compelling when talking about his form, his confidence, his status as inspiration of the team and whatever pressure that comes with it.

"The nature of the beast is, at club and country, you have a lot of responsibility, a lot of weight on your shoulders," he said. "When you do something well, you're the best thing since sliced bread. When you don't have a great couple of games, or you're not producing assists, or you make a poor pass in a pivotal moment of the game, you're automatically not good enough.

"It's the nature of being my age (he'll be 32 later in the month). It's the nature of competing with Scotland and with Aston Villa. I take the praise with a big smile. Any criticism that comes, it's just part of it."

McGinn's influence for his country has probably reduced from the mighty highs of before. None of the pride and passion and phenomenal work-rate has gone, but the game-defining moments have not been there, save for the odd glimpse.

Pocognoli not feeling pressure for first Scotland win

Robertson's Scotland career in numbers as 100th cap looms

Haiti, and the double deflection, sticks out, but beyond that, McGinn has been too quiet for too long. It's unfair to saddle him with the expectation of being superman every time he plays, but he's the one who fans look to, his is the name they chant in good times and in bad.

His last Scotland goal before Haiti at the World Cup was coming up for two years ago.

Opproprium will rein down for the mere mention of him being under pressure to deliver, of course. Being McGinn, he could dominate and score in Skopje, but a reminder of his talent is overdue.

You ask if he feels, as a 91-cap colossus, undroppable. "No, no. I'm certainly not undroppable, " he replied. "I remember Steve Clarke put me on the bench and I had absolutely no issue with that.

"I don't think anyone in the squad is undroppable. It's the challenge to anyone coming into the squad and I encourage that challenge.

"The competition is always there, whether that's someone who's 20, 21 or in their 30s. The best players will play for Scotland. If the manager said to me, 'You're on the bench, I need you for five minutes, ten minutes, zero minutes or 90-plus', we're here to represent Scotland.

"The thing that's made us so successful over the years is that it doesn't matter if you play for Aston Villa, Motherwell, Hibs, St Mirren, anyone. You represent Scotland and at the end of the day the best team will take to the pitch.

"If that's a team without me in it, I'll be the biggest Scotland supporter on the bench."

What keeps him driving on? He's quick to answer. "What keeps me going is how I felt on that first night (his 2016 debut) against Denmark - the pride, the emotion. When you're picked to play for your country, you never know when it's going to be your last, so you don't take it for granted.

"Quite possibly tomorrow night, you never know. It could be the last time you're chosen."

McGinn, of course, has glorious history and iconic status with St Mirren and Hibs, but at Villa something extra-special has happened. His status is now deeply rooted as a legend of the club. Talk to their fans and it's not an appraisal you get but a hagiography. Understandably.

McGinn (more than most others) was the one who got them out of the Championship in 2019, the one who kept them in the Premier League in 2020, the one who dragged them from 17th to 11th to 14th to 7th to 4th in the English top flight, the one who helped bring Champions League football, the one who captained them and scored for them when winning a European trophy last season, the one who broke their European goalscoring record.

McGinn was one of the ones who stayed. Jack Grealish didn't, Douglas Luiz didn't, Ollie Watkins didn't, Emi Martinez didn't, Youri Tielemans didn't.

The best Villa captain since Dennis Mortimer, some say. Given that Mortimer was leader of the iconic league winning team of 1981 and the European Cup winning side of 1982 then that's some compliment.

What makes a legend, somebody asked recently in a Villa discussion. "Humility", "determination", "tenacity", "leadership", "longevity", "success." One club diehard wrote that they've had loads of players in recent decades who tick some of those boxes but it takes a special individual to tick all of them - "and McGinn does."

As one observer put it: "He's unquestionably ahead of any other player we've had this century and surpasses some of the legends from the last one, too." Another said that he fully expects his infant son to say to him in later life: "What was it like watching John McGinn?"

He's too long in the tooth now to be overly influenced by praise or flak. "If I was younger, I would have been straight on Instagram or straight on Twitter," he added. "Everyone's entitled to their opinion, but at the end of the day, you keep your head down, you keep working hard.

"If you go through a barren spell or you go through a spell where you're not doing too well, you need to find that inner self-belief, which I feel like I have. The older you get, you learn how to manage tough moments better. They get worse, though.

"The lows get lower and the highs become less high. But you certainly deal with it a lot better when you're older. When you're younger, it completely consumes you and you try and work too hard to come out of what could potentially be a difficult moment. But I feel as if I'm managing those times well.

"As you get older, you think, 'Oh, can I keep doing this?' But it certainly makes the good days a lot better. You know after a game like Switzerland, do you turn the telly on? No. Do you listen to radio reports? Nope. But if it's 3-0 to Scotland, I would be lying if I said I wouldn't listen to some of it."

The prospect of following in Robertson's footsteps is an enormous incentive. Eight to go after North Macedonia.

More fireworks to come, you hope. Compared to the huge moments in past seasons, McGinn might be in a bit of an international lull right now, but is there a single soul out there who thinks he's done with the heroics? In the tartan-clad city of Teresa, few, you fancy, have lost belief.

articles.title: Nations League: Robert Lewandowski scores hat-trick and Edin Dzeko retires
articles.summary: Robert Lewandowski, 38, scores a hat-trick in the Nations League and Edin Dzeko plays his final game for Bosnia-Herzegovina.
articles.body:
Robert Lewandowski scored a hat-trick as Poland thrashed 10-man Romania 6-0 in the Nations League.

After Tottenham defender Radu Dragusin, who is on loan at Fiorentina, was sent off in the 22nd minute, Romania were dismantled in Warsaw.

Lewandowski opened the scoring from the penalty spot and doubled the lead early in the second half.

An own goal and strikes from Piotr Zielinski and Jan Bednarek followed before 38-year-old Lewandowski completed his seventh international hat-trick.

The former Barcelona striker has scored 92 international goals.

Poland are third in Group B4, while Romania stay fourth.

Gheorghe Hagi, in his second spell in charge, became the first Romania manager to lose his first three competitive matches.

In the same group there were emotional scenes as Edin Dzeko retired from international football following Bosnia-Herzegovina's 1-1 draw at home to Sweden.

The ex-Manchester City forward, 40, found the net late in the first half but the goal was disallowed as the ball went out of play in the build-up.

Fireworks went off after 11 minutes to celebrate the number 11 on his 152nd international appearance, and he was given a standing ovation when he was substituted after 62 minutes in Zenica.

The celebrations continued after the match with an official ceremony, a guard of honour and a drone show displaying messages of thanks to Dzeko, who was showered with soft toys from the crowd during a lap of honour.

Arsenal striker Viktor Gyokeres put Sweden in front before Kerim Alajbegovic equalised for Bosnia-Herzegovina.

Kevin de Bruyne scored twice as Belgium beat Turkey 3-0 to move up to second in Group A1.

The 35-year-old Napoli midfielder scored a goal in each half before Romelu Lukaku completed the scoring.

Liverpool defender Milos Kerkez scored the only goal as Hungary beat Georgia in Budapest to claim their first Nations League win of the campaign.

Hungary are third in Group B2, three points behind leaders Northern Ireland.

articles.summary: El delantero de 41 años reaccionó a una publicación que criticaba a sus compañeros por la falta de apoyo y respeto que le habían demostrado en los últimos días
articles.body: El capítulo de Cristiano Ronaldo con la Selección está lejos de cerrarse. Pese a que Portugal ha firmado tres victorias en esta Nations League, la polémica alrededor de la salida del delantero de la concentración continúa creciendo. Y ahora hay un nuevo elemento que ha vuelto a encender los ánimos en Portugal: el 'me gusta' del propio Cristiano a unas declaraciones muy críticas con sus compañeros. El protagonista de esas palabras fue Felipe Melo, exfutbolista brasileño, que cargó contra la actitud de los futbolistas portugueses con su capitán. El brasileño cuestionó públicamente la falta de apoyo y respeto hacia el delantero de 41 años en unas declaraciones para Sportv. El vídeo terminó en Instagram y rápidamente se hizo viral. Acumula más de 27.000 'me gusta', pero hubo uno que no pasó desapercibido: el de Cristiano. Un gesto aparentemente sencillo que ha vuelto a poner el foco sobre la relación entre el capitán y el resto del vestuario portugués y que está generando malestar y debate en el país. Felipe Melo había puesto sobre la mesa una comparación especialmente sensible. Según el brasileño, existe una diferencia notable entre cómo los compañeros de Ronaldo le tratan a él y cómo los futbolistas argentinos respaldan a Lionel Messi. Además, utilizó a Hojlund para ilustrar hasta qué punto el portugués sigue siendo una referencia para otros jugadores. "Hay una diferencia grotesca en la forma en que sus compañeros portugueses tratan a Cristiano y los jugadores argentinos tratan a Lionel Messi", comenzó diciendo. Melo también destacó el respeto que, a su juicio, Ronaldo continúa despertando entre sus propios rivales. "Veo mucho más respeto en los rivales cuando juegan contra Cristiano Ronaldo, y ayer Hojlund se enfadó mucho con Jorge Jesus porque su ídolo es Cristiano Ronaldo, en lugar de la selección portuguesa. Eso está mal, porque allí nadie se acerca a los tobillos de Cristiano Ronaldo. No se le puede dejar salir así como si nada hubiera pasado", dijo. El hecho de que Cristiano haya dado "me gusta" precisamente a este mensaje añade todavía más gasolina a un asunto que parecía destinado a apagarse tras sus tres victorias con Portugal. Su gesto, aunque no vaya acompañado de ninguna declaración, ha reabierto el debate sobre lo ocurrido en la concentración y vuelve a colocar al capitán en el centro de la conversación.

articles.title: La final no nos la tienen que dar, si acaso nos la tendrían que quitar

articles.body: Aficiones Unidas empapeló La Cartuja con bufandas reclamando la final del Mundial 2030 para nuestro país. Louzán intensifica su mensaje de que será en España. Alejandro Blanco expresó que no se entendería el Mundial sin que la final fuera aquí. Pero Martínez Almeida no es tan optimista y recela cada vez más de Casablanca. Marruecos sigue trabajando bien entre bambalinas. Aquí veo todo demasiado en pañales aún. En medio de las dudas, la frase más certera se la he escuchado a Sonia Cea: “La final no nos la tienen que dar, si acaso nos la tendrían que quitar”. Tiene toda la razón. Lo que toca es defender esa posición y luchar para que no nos la arrebaten. § El ‘Caso Negreira’ no puede cerrarse sin consecuencias. Eso todo el mundo lo sabe. El Madrid ha sacado los tanques (que tuvo guardados mientras el Barça le siguió el juego con la fracasada Superliga) y los ha aparcado en la puerta de la UEFA. Supongo que reactivar el caso es una de las condiciones para retomar la relación con el máximo organismo. § Hacía mucho tiempo que la selección no despertaba tanta expectación más allá de los grandes torneos. Además del talento del equipo y del tirón espectacular de Lamine, el mérito indiscutible de esto es de Luis de la Fuente. Por cierto, su Balón de Oro también es indiscutible, ¿no? § Cristiano Ronaldo no puede cerrar de este modo tan agrio su brillante historia con la selección portuguesa. § Aguardando la sentencia al Manchester City, que puede y debe ser descomunal, recuerdo que Javier Tebas fue el primero que denunció la desventaja que suponía competir contra los Clubes Estado. § Cestero, Asencio, Valverde... Me gusta el olor a scoop en MARCA por las mañanas. § ¡Ya está aquí el Hyatlón! § Fabián Ruiz no sabe perder. Propongo que el equipo de casa elija campo o saque. Y ya está. § Periodistas que dan lecciones pero ninguna noticia.

articles.title: Man City whistleblower Pinto to lose witness protection amid death threats
articles.summary: Pinto says he will go into hiding for an indefinite period following the Premier League’s guilty verdict against City.
articles.body:
Computer hacker Rui Pinto , the whistleblower whose leaks triggered an investigation into Manchester City Football Club, says he fears for his life after being told that his witness protection would end on October 10.

Pinto wrote in a social media post on Friday that he has received “multiple death threats” and he would move to an undisclosed location over fears for his life.

“Given these circumstances, I have no alternative but to relocate, within the next few days, to an undisclosed location for an indefinite period of time, due to the multiple death threats I have received and the serious risk of an assassination attempt against me,” Pinto wrote on X.

Pinto said he was informed on Wednesday that his witness protection programme from Portuguese authorities would end on October 10, “thereby knowingly placing me in a life-threatening situation”.

The 37-year-old Portuguese founder of the website Football Leaks obtained private documents that showed City broke league rules from 2009 to 2018. An independent commission found City guilty of all but one of 115 charges brought against them over breaches of Premier League financial rules.

On Friday, City filed an appeal against the ruling as it seeks to overturn the decision and avoid potentially severe sanctions.

Pinto, a self-taught hacker and activist who has exposed some of the biggest scandals in football, has been a protected witness since August 2020 after agreeing to grant Portuguese authorities access to millions of files gathered before his arrest. His first trial in Portugal began a month later. He was given a suspended sentence for illegally obtaining documents, committing other cybercrimes and attempted extortion

He has been vociferous about City’s financial misconduct scandal on social media since the commission’s verdict was first reported last week. He has called the ruling a “historic decision for English football”.

“For this reason, I have just set up a GoFundMe campaign and I am asking for everyone’s support to help me survive this serious situation created by the Portuguese State, which, as I have already stated, has knowingly decided to place my life at risk.”

Pinto added his thanks to everyone who supported Football Leaks, which he founded in 2015 under the pseudonym “John” before being unmasked in 2019.

“I can give everyone one guarantee: the fight will most certainly continue!”

Hours before Pinto’s post on Friday, his lawyers said he faces “dire consequences” after being told his witness protection would end.

Pinto “was informed on Wednesday that the special security programme he has benefited from since August 2020 would end on October 10″, his Portuguese lawyers Francisco and Luisa Teixeira da Mota said in a joint statement with his French representatives William Bourdon and Vincent Brengarth.

“In a few days, without having been given a prior hearing as required by law, he would lose the secure, confidential housing assigned to him and be forced to find a new home urgently, with no guarantee that police protection would be maintained,” they continued, describing the move as a “decision with dire consequences”.

“The threats against him are not merely theoretical; he was assaulted in Lisbon last April. His revelations implicated powerful figures with vast resources, and numerous resulting legal proceedings are still ongoing,” they noted.

“Abruptly deprived of his protected housing and plunged into extreme precariousness, Rui Pinto is reportedly more vulnerable now than at any time since 2020,” his lawyers added.

articles.title: Caso Manchester City: el colonialismo cambia de sentido
articles.standfirst: El deporte fue una importante vía de propaganda y penetración cultural... y lo sigue siendo
articles.summary: El deporte fue una importante vía de propaganda y penetración cultural... y lo sigue siendo
articles.body: El colonialismo y el imperialismo siempre han existido. En la segunda mitad del siglo XIX fueron los países que antes se industrializaron quienes más y 'mejor' practicaron esta particular modalidad de relaciones internacionales. Esquemáticamente, se basaba en que cuando un país con la suficiente potencia militar y económica encontraba un territorio del que entendía que podía extraer rendimiento, lo ocupaba de grado o por fuerza y procedía a explotarlo. Esta 'ocupación' podía desarrollarse según variadas formas. No siempre era imperativa la sustitución de las estructuras políticas. En realidad y con lógica se escogía la forma de dominio menos onerosa para la potencia colonial, y en ello tenía también parte la influencia cultural. Si nos centramos en el Imperio Británico, el más extenso y exitoso -para la metrópoli- de la época, junto a las cañoneras y acorazados de la Royal Navy, los fusiles Martini-Henry y los Casacas Rojas estaba también la propaganda. Y en ella tenía un importante papel una actividad recientemente 'inventada' en las Islas Británicas: el 'sport'. En este siglo XIX del que hablamos en el Reino Unido se habían inventado, o al menos desarrollado y reglamentado, actividades como el foot-ball, el lawn-tennis, el golf, el boxing, el cricket y alguna modalidad más. Y no se ocultaba -más bien se destacaba- que la conversión de juegos en deportes reglamentados era también una forma de educación. En origen, para la propia sociedad -una sociedad muy clasista, pero eso es otra historia- pero rápidamente sus impulsores se dieron cuenta de que también podían valer para 'educar' a otros a la manera británica, o inculcarles veladamente un concepto de superioridad cultural. Si se trataba de esto, las modas vendrían de París pero el 'sport', que empezaba a ser actividad de primera importancia mundial, venía de Londres: los reglamentos y el material, que se compraba en Lillywhite's. Y eso significaba reconocer de facto la superioridad británica en una actividad que rápidamente ganó popularidad mundial. Sí. El deporte era una via de penetración cultural. Pacífica. Los diplomáticos y comerciantes británicos no perdían la ocasión de acrecentar el prestigio y el atractivo del Imperio con partidos de foot-ball para las clases populares o elegantes sesiones de lawn-tennis, concursos hípicos, o explicando cómo se podía disponer algún paraje para jugar al golf para los potentados locales. A veces se hacía apostolado. Otras veces simplemente los locales trataban de acercarse e imitar los usos y costumbres de los 'maestros'. Y el Imperio ganaba prestigio. La era de colonialismo occidental directo acabó a mediados del siglo XX. Y por no extendernos mucho, señalaremos que hubo colonizados que comprendieron los resortes de la actividad y, cuando pudieron, los usaron. Y, recordemos, uno de esos resortes, uno de los más efectivos, fue la penetración cultural a través del deporte. Vamos ahora a finales del siglo XX y principios del XXI. El dominio de la producción y suministro de petróleo fue un objetivo tardío del colonialismo pero acabó volviéndose el más importante. Cuando hubo de ponerse fin al colonialismo clásico las 'potencias' hicieron lo posible por seguir, en la práctica, manejándolo, pero la Crisis del Petróleo de 1973 demostró que quien ahora lo poseía se había dado perfecta cuenta de su poder. De un modo u otro seguimos viviendo consecuencias de aquel momento. Y el mecanismo del colonialismo seguía vigente. La potencia militar ya no entraba directamente en la ecuación pero, a cambio, el capital ganaba mucha importancia. Y algunos estados antaño directa o indirectamente colonizados ahora, a caballo de la riqueza petrolera, tenían mucho dinero. Suficiente para, si querían, reproducir antiguos esquemas. La Humanidad tiene cinco lenguajes comunes: dinero, política, arte, sexo y deporte. Y el deporte tiene elementos de todos los demás. A finales del XIX y principios del XX vimos como una serie de estados con ciertas dificultades para ser admitidos en los estándares del Primer Mundo -que requiere, además de riqueza, cierto grado de desarrollo humano y derechos individuales- se apercibieron de que el deporte seguía siendo una gran herramienta de penetración cultural y de mejora de imagen. Un deporte que, además se había desarrollado muchísimo como negocio. Dos y dos siguen siendo cuatro. En poco tiempo empezamos a ver Juegos Olímpicos en China, Fórmula 1 en Rusia, mundiales de fútbol en el Golfo Pérsico, candidaturas olímpicas sólidamente respaldadas, regias sedes de competiciones de cualquier deporte, modernísimas instalaciones de ensueño y un maná económico sobre el deporte procedente de eso que se dio en llamar 'el petrodólar': inversiones en infraestructura, inversiones en clubes -de fútbol, sobre todo- y competiciones, patrocinios, circuitos de golf de nuevo cuño, exhibiciones fastuosas... Pero en estas ha llegado el caso del Manchester City, como en su día llego a menor escala del PSG. Tienen a mano los detalles. El club, que creció exponencialmente con dinero inyectado desde Emiratos Árabes, es ahora reo de haber cometido mil irregularidades que le pueden llevar a una seria sanción. En el Reino Unido se ha constatado que los financiadores emiratíes no han colaborado demasiado en las investigaciones. Y desde Emiratos se ha dicho que si esa sanción es muy dura se pueden comprometer futuras inversiones en la economía británica: es decir que exigen que se respete su forma de hacer las cosas, que es la que ya vemos. ¿Les suena el modo de actuación? No hay cañoneras ni regimientos ni ametralladoras Gatling... pero hay millones. Quizá haya a quien le tome por sorpresa enterarse de que todo ese dinero que llovía del cielo sobre la industria del deporte no era, en realidad, gratis. Juzgue cada cual si podía o puede tener una finalidad fácilmente equiparable a aquella penetración cultural de hace unos 150 años y si el colonialismo, impulsado ahora más por el capital que por las cañoneras -al menos en algunos sitios- ha cambiado de sentido. El hecho es que después del 'festival' de hace 20 años ahora empiezan a retirarse inversiones como las del riquísimo LIV Golf saudí, mientras otras tienen, como vemos, problemas. Al final, la historia no se detiene…

articles.title: Matarazzo: "Es importante que futbolistas que llevaban tiempo sin jugar hayan tenido muchos minutos"
articles.standfirst: El técnico de la Real reconoció el triunfo justo del Athletic y sacó una lectura positiva
articles.summary: El técnico de la Real reconoció el triunfo justo del Athletic y sacó una lectura positiva
articles.body: Pellegrino Matarazzo consideró que el Athletic de Bilbao ganó con justicia a su Real Sociedad en la final de la ‘Euskal Herria Txapela’, un partido que sirvió para que algunos de sus futbolistas tuvieran los minutos de los que no están disfrutando en LaLiga. Matarazzo no puso peros al triunfo del Athletic. “Fue un partido difícil, en el que el Athletic fue el mejor equipo, le felicito por la victoria. Creo que empezamos bien, pero luego tuvimos muchas pérdidas que rompieron nuestro ritmo. Y cuando presionamos arriba, nos cansamos, porque perseguimos el balón y sin peligro con balón no generamos lo suficiente. Perdimos por un gol en balón parado, pero fue merecido”. Se le comentó que a su equipo le faltó hacer más daño en ataque. “Sí, estoy de acuerdo. Teníamos a Gonçalo, que a veces estaba ahí, a veces no. También a Zakharyan, que hizo un buen partido, pese a que no siempre estuvo preciso en sus pases pero, si quieres dominar el centro del campo, necesitas un juego diferente, tuvimos demasiadas pérdidas fáciles que nos restaron confianza y eso lo hizo más difícil”. Matarazzo miró el lado positivo de las hasta 11 bajas que tuvo, cuando le dijeron que habían podido influir en la derrota. “Posibilitaron que cinco futbolistas que llevaban mucho tiempo sin competir lo pudieran hacer, como Aihen, Zakharyan, Rupérez y algunos más. Han tenido muchos minutos de competición y es muy importante. Pero en el Athletic también pasó algo así, es normal en un partido como este, así que no hay excusas”. Por ello, el técnico txuriurdin entendió la falta de conexión a veces entre sus jugadores. “Es normal. Cuando juegan 11 jugadores juntos en el campo se entienden mejor, los automatismos están más establecidos y la sensación de que nos faltó eso la tuvimos, porque era la primera vez que muchos jugadores jugaban juntos. Pero el Athletic tuvo un problema parecido, quizás la diferencia estuvo en la manera de construir el juego”. Matarazzo fue cuestionado por el de nuevo cargado calendario que le espera a su equipo a la vuelta del parón internacional, en el que participan hasta nueve de sus futbolistas. "Siempre es importante mantenerse sano. Sí que son muchos partidos y entiendo que es importante que los futbolistas descansen bien, empezando por los que vuelvan de las selecciones. Somos conscientes de que ellos también tienen que tener sus momentos de descanso y lo tenemos en mente, vamos a ver como buscamos el equilibrio para que todos estén con un buen nivel de forma y con hambre de jugar”. En ese sentido, el de Nueva Jersey se congratuló de que esté habiendo pocas lesiones en su plantilla. "Estoy muy contento en ese sentido de como hemos hecho las cosas en la pretemporada, porque hemos tenido muy pocas lesiones. La de Marín, que hoy ha vuelto a jugar, y la de Zubeldia, que regresará a los entrenamientos la próxima semana, una buena noticia

articles.title: Turkish court detains football refereeing chief pending corruption trial
articles.summary: Seven officials face an investigation over allegations of manipulation of the referee administration process.
articles.body:
The head of Turkiye’s football refereeing body and four other officials have been placed in pretrial detention by a court as part of a corruption investigation , the state news agency Anadolu reports.

Ferhat Gundogdu, head of the Central Referees Committee, and six others appeared before a judge over allegations of manipulation of the referee administration process, Anadolu said on Saturday.

They appeared on Friday before a judge at Istanbul’s Caglayan courthouse on several charges, including forgery of official documents, breach of trust and illegal acquisition of personal data, the report said.

The judge remanded five people in custody and granted the other two conditional release, Anadolu said.

It was the latest scandal to shake football in Turkiye, coming exactly a year after the Turkish Football Federation (TFF) suspended 149 referees on charges of illegal betting.

On Thursday night, police from the illegal betting and sports crime unit also detained Yasin Kol, a referee from Turkiye’s top-flight Super Lig, as well as an assistant referee, media reports said.

Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said prosecutors are examining claims about “interference in the processes of referee classification, assignments, scoring and appointments as well as the exams on rules”.

During raids on Tuesday, police searched the VAR room at TFF’s headquarters in Istanbul. Observers said the investigation was likely linked to last year’s betting scandal and would have implications for the federation.

“It does seem to be a continuation of 2025, and it looks like it will continue further,” sports journalist Ayhan Sensoy told the AFP news agency.

Sensoy, who wrote a 2024 book on the issue called The Gambling Pit, said it was unlikely that federation bosses “have any chance of staying in office”.

So far, the TFF has not directly addressed the arrests as its top officials are due to fly home on Saturday after attending Friday night’s Belgium-Turkiye UEFA Nations League clash in Liege, which Turkiye lost 3-0.
